articles.title: Economic worries abound ahead of Brazil runoff
articles.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
articles.summary: Economic worries are feeding voter discontent ahead of Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday, helping the conservative challenger’s prospects. Once defined by the size and strength of its labor movement, the number of unionized workers in Latin America’s biggest economy has shrunk by almost half in the last 15 or so years. That shift is partly explained by the rise in gig work: Almost two million Brazilians now work full-time for transport or delivery apps. The loss of worker protection has fed discontent, with almost 50% of respondents to a September poll saying the economy had worsened in the last year. In response, leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva this week fast-tracked welfare payments as he looks to catch up in the polls. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

stories.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said protests not organized by trade unions would be banned, as the Élysée braces for further unrest ahead of demonstrations planned for Saturday. French cities have been shaken in recent weeks by vandalism and looting sparked by cost-of-living demonstrations, amid a broader crisis besieging the country’s lame-duck centrist government that has spiked French bond yields. In the face of deficits and discontent, Europe’s “ centrists seem out of ideas ,” The Economist argued, while far-right and -left parties seize opportunity from chaos. “ Politics is not a spectator sport ,” the founder of a new Spanish political party wrote, calling for “a center that stops being the guardian of the status quo and runs towards the future at speed.” — Brendan Ruberry
